forbids: an intake that changes anything before a person assesses — a requirement state, a count, a rendered page or a policy record — and an intake that puts a document in force without a human approving it
note: Registered with the feature (BL-240). The property is borrowed verbatim from vendor-register/SKILL.md: 'the reading layer changed NOTHING… If proposing ever moves the count, something is wrong.' The two halves are the two ways an intake breaks it: by writing a record on sight, or by writing one that is already in force.

mutations.why: `ingest` creates the policy record directly instead of a proposal — the single most likely 'improvement' anyone makes to this code, because it looks like removing a pointless extra step for a user who has just handed the tool a hundred documents. It is not a pointless step: it is the entire boundary between a reading and a record. Under this mutation the read model MOVES, requirement rows appear, and a CISO who ingested a shelf of policies to see what was in them has silently populated their register with rows nobody assessed.
defeats: ingesting documents leaves the WHOLE read model byte-identical
mutations.replace:
add_policy(store, st["title"], st["owner"], version=st["version"])
        rec = dict(st, id=next_proposal_id(store), status=PROPOSAL_OPEN,

mutations.why: THE SUPERSESSION PROPERTY, and it is structural rather than checked — which is exactly why a mutation is needed to show the structure is load-bearing. `assess` confirms straight to `approved` instead of leaving a draft. Nothing raises, the record looks complete, and the citation is still attached. What is gone is the guarantee: a batch confirming a v3.0 document would put it in force alongside the v2.0 it replaces, for the same requirements, with nothing recording which governs — the exact state `approve` already refuses when a human reaches it, arriving through the one door that does not go past that refusal.
defeats: a confirmed proposal creates a DRAFT, never an approved record
